faq.a: No, E. coli is a non‑pathogenic commensal; only E. histolytica is invasive.
It clears tissue trophozoites but does not eradicate cysts in the lumen, leading to relapse.
Amebic abscess is usually solitary, right‑lobe, with normal white‑cell count; pyogenic often multiple, left‑lobe, and high neutrophils.
faq.q: What distinguishes an amebic liver abscess from a pyogenic one?

exam: A 25‑year‑old farmer presents with bloody diarrhea and right‑upper‑quadrant pain – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Order stool microscopy and an abdominal ultrasound; microscopy confirms invasive disease, ultrasound detects possible liver abscess.

How does the life cycle of Entamoeba histolytica explain the need for a luminal drug after metronidazole? — Cysts survive in the lumen after tissue parasites are killed; paromomycin eradicates them to prevent recurrence.

A patient with a liver lesion has a normal bilirubin; what condition does this suggest and what is the first‑line therapy? — Suggests amebic liver abscess; treat with metronidazole followed by paromomycin.

Why is nitroimidazole contraindicated in late pregnancy for amebiasis? — Metronidazole crosses the placenta and is associated with teratogenicity in the first trimester; safer alternatives are limited, so treat after delivery if possible.

In a setting without imaging, how would you differentiate amebic from bacterial dysentery clinically? — Look for mucus‑filled blood‑streaked stool, low-grade fever, and absence of high leukocytosis; bacterial dysentery often has high fever and leukocytosis.
What are the key public‑health measures to prevent amebiasis in a refugee camp? — Provide safe drinking water, promote hand washing with soap, ensure proper latrine use, and educate on food hygiene.

A child with amebic dysentery develops severe dehydration; what immediate management is required? — Initiate oral rehydration solution or IV fluids if unable to tolerate oral intake, monitor electrolytes, and start metronidazole promptly.

How would you explain a false‑negative stool microscopy result? — Intermittent shedding of cysts, inadequate sample size, or poor preservation can miss organisms; repeat testing or use antigen detection.
ai.title: Entamoeba histolytica Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic dysentery and liver abscess, common in low‑resource tropical settings. Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy, antigen tests or imaging; treatment is metronidazole followed by a luminal agent.

b: Peak incidence in children and young adults
sections.p: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite transmitted via the fecal‑oral route, thriving in areas with poor sanitation. It can remain asymptomatic or cause invasive disease of the colon and liver.

b: Cyst: 4 nuclei, 10‑12 µm, resistant to chlorine
sections.p: A flagellated, anaerobic protozoan that exists as a cyst (infective) and trophozoite (invasive). Cysts survive outside the host for weeks in moist environments.
Ingestion of mature cysts from contaminated water, food or hands leads to excystation in the ileum, colonisation of the colon, and possible invasion into the bloodstream.

b: Colitis: bloody stools, abdominal cramps, fever
Liver abscess: right‑upper‑quadrant pain, fever, hepatomegaly
sections.p: Two major clinical syndromes: amebic dysentery (colitis) and amebic liver abscess. Extra‑hepatic spread can involve lungs, brain, or peritoneum.

b: If microscopy unavailable, send stool for antigen test to a regional lab
When imaging not possible, diagnose liver abscess clinically and treat empirically
sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with laboratory and imaging. In low‑resource settings, rely on microscopy; where available, use antigen detection or PCR.

t.b: Detects trophozoites or cysts; confirms infection when seen in ≥3 specimens
Answers whether E. histolytica is present; positive result is highly specific
Answers if a liver lesion is present; a solitary hypoechoic lesion with peripheral rim suggests abscess
Answers if exposure has occurred; positive in >90 % of liver abscesses but may stay positive after cure

b: Avoid chloroquine (ineffective) and nitrofurantoin (poor tissue penetration)
sections.p: Eradicate invasive trophozoites first, then eliminate luminal cysts to prevent relapse. Emphasise safe water, hand hygiene, and food safety.

b: Amebic dysentery: mucus‑filled blood‑streaked stool, no high fever
Liver abscess: solitary right‑lobe lesion, normal bilirubin
Metronidazole followed by paromomycin is mandatory
sections.p: Focus on distinguishing amebic from bacterial dysentery, recognizing liver abscess without jaundice, and knowing the two‑step therapy.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status)
Perforation: sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen
